unit.title: Shares
unit.description: What you buy with a share, how you get dividends and what kinds of companies there are

steps.title: Owning a tiny slice
steps.body:
A company is divided into **shares**. Inditex has around 3,100 million: if you buy one, you own a minuscule part of its shops, its brands and its future profits.

That's why they're called **equities** (variable income): what you make isn't fixed, it depends on how the business does.

steps.title: Why companies sell shares
steps.body:
To raise money without taking out loans. When they **go public** (an IPO) they sell part of the company to investors, who share in its profits and its risks.

After that, shares are bought and sold **between investors**: the company no longer receives that money.

steps.title: Where your returns come from
steps.body: **Total return = dividends + capital gains.** In the long run the price follows profits; in the short run, expectations move it. If the company goes bust, shareholders get paid last and almost never get anything back.
steps.key: A share is a slice of a business: you make money if the business earns more and pays out or grows.
steps.tip: Buying a share is buying a business, not a number that goes up and down.

steps.title: Three kinds of rights
steps.body:
• **Economic:** receiving dividends if they're paid and your share if the company is sold or wound up.
• **Voting:** voting at the **annual general meeting** (board, accounts, directors' pay…).
• **Information:** receiving the accounts and relevant information.

And a very useful one: **pre-emptive rights** in capital increases.

steps.title: Your vote weighs what your shares weigh
steps.body:
As a general rule, **one share = one vote**. With 10 shares in a bank that has billions of them, your vote counts for very little, but you can vote remotely or appoint a proxy.

The big funds really do swing votes. Some companies have **non-voting** shares or give double votes to people who hold them for years.

steps.title: Information for everyone at once
steps.body: Listed companies must publish their accounts and report any **inside information** (results, acquisitions, problems) to the **CNMV** so that all investors learn about it at the same time.
steps.key: Being a shareholder gives you economic, voting and information rights, in proportion to your shares.
steps.tip: The accounts of every Spanish listed company are free on the CNMV website.

u8l3.title: Dividends: how and when you get paid

steps.title: A dividend's dates
steps.body:
1. **Announcement:** the company says how much it'll pay.
2. **Ex-dividend date:** from that day on, the share trades **without** the right to that dividend.
3. **Record date:** they check who the shareholders are.
4. **Payment date:** the money reaches your account.

To get it, you need to hold the share **before** the ex-dividend date.

steps.title: Why the price drops
steps.body:
On the ex-dividend date the price drops by roughly the amount paid out: if a share is worth €20 and pays €0.50, it'll open at around €19.50.

You haven't got any richer: you have €0.50 in cash and €0.50 less in shares. And in Spain dividends are taxed: the payer already **withholds 19 %**.

steps.title: Dividend yield
steps.body: **Dividend yield = annual dividend ÷ price.** A €30 share that pays €1.20 a year yields 4 %. Careful: a sky-high dividend is sometimes a warning that the price has fallen because a cut is expected.
steps.key: A dividend isn't free money: it comes out of the company's value.
steps.tip: A sky-high dividend is sometimes an alarm bell, not a gift.

u8l4.title: Splits, reverse splits and capital increases

steps.title: Split: more slices, same pizza
steps.body:
In a **split** the company divides each share into several. If you have 10 shares at €400 and there's a 4-for-1 split, you end up with **40 shares at €100**. You still have €4,000.

It's done to make the share more manageable. Apple (4-for-1 in 2020) and NVIDIA (10-for-1 in 2024) both did it.

steps.title: Reverse split and capital increase
steps.body:
• **Reverse split:** the other way round, shares are combined. 1,000 shares at €0.20 with a 1-for-10 become 100 at €2. It's usually done by companies whose price has fallen a lot.
• **Capital increase:** the company **issues new shares** to raise money. If you don't take part, your percentage falls: that's **dilution**.

steps.title: What changes and what doesn't
steps.body: Splits and reverse splits only change the number of slices. A capital increase does change the cake: new money and more owners come in. Some Spanish companies pay the dividend in new shares if you want (the *scrip* or flexible dividend).
steps.key: Cutting the pizza into more slices doesn't give you more pizza.
steps.tip: If a headline says «the share plunges 75 %», check first whether there's been a split.

steps.title: Market capitalisation
steps.body:
**Market cap = price × number of shares.** It's what the company is worth on the stock market.

A common convention (in dollars):
• **Large caps:** over 10,000 million.
• **Mid caps:** from 2,000 to 10,000 million.
• **Small caps:** from 300 to 2,000 million.
• Below that, *micro caps*.

steps.title: Risk and potential
steps.body:
**Small caps** can grow far more (a 500 million company can multiply in value; a giant hardly can), but they're more volatile, less liquid (wider *spreads*) and go bust more often.

**Large caps** are more stable and hundreds of analysts follow them.

steps.title: Indices by size
steps.body: The S&P 500 and IBEX 35 bring together large companies. The Russell 2000, small US ones. In Spain there are the IBEX Medium Cap and IBEX Small Cap. A global index is cap-weighted: the giants weigh most.
steps.key: Smaller = more potential, but also more volatility and more risk of going bust.
steps.tip: Being small doesn't make a company cheap or good: just riskier.

steps.title: Two styles
steps.body:
• **Growth:** companies whose sales and profits are growing fast. They reinvest almost everything and pay little or no dividend. They look **expensive** relative to what they earn today.
• **Value:** mature companies that look **cheap** relative to their profits or their net assets. They usually pay a dividend.

steps.title: The P/E at a glance
steps.body:
**P/E = price ÷ earnings per share.** How many years of current earnings you're paying for.

A €100 share earning €2 per share has a P/E of 50: the market expects a lot of growth. A €40 one earning €5, a P/E of 8.

You'll look at it in depth in the fundamental analysis section.

steps.title: Neither always wins
steps.body: Each style has its good periods. The risk with growth: if it disappoints, a high P/E deflates in one go. The risk with value: sometimes cheap is cheap for a reason (the **value trap**).
steps.key: Growth: you pay today for future earnings. Value: you buy current earnings at a discount.
steps.tip: A great company isn't always a great investment: it depends on the price you pay.

steps.title: What a buyback is
steps.body:
The company uses its cash to **buy its own shares** on the market and, usually, **cancel them** (destroy them). Fewer shares are left, so each one represents a bigger slice of the business and of the profits.

Apple has been buying back shares since 2012, to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars.

steps.title: The maths
steps.body:
A company earns 500 million and has 100 million shares: **€5 of earnings per share (EPS)**. If it buys back and cancels 10 million, the same profit is shared among 90 million: **€5.56** per share, 11 % more.

Your percentage goes up without you putting in a single euro.

steps.title: Dividend or buyback
steps.body: Both return money to shareholders. A dividend reaches you in cash and is taxed that year; a buyback increases your stake and you only pay tax when you sell. But buying back at a **high price** destroys value, and doing it with debt adds risk.
steps.key: A buyback shares the cake among fewer owners.
steps.tip: Always ask what price the company is buying back at: buying expensive isn't returning value.

u8l1-1.prompt: You buy an Inditex share. What are you?
options: Co-owner of a minuscule part of the company
A customer with a discount in its shops
u8l1-1.explanation: A share is part of the company's capital: you share in its profits and its risks. Lending money to the company would mean buying a bond.

u8l1-2.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u8l1-2.explanation: These are the four basic words of equity investing: what you buy, how it gets onto the stock market and where your returns come from.
right: Stock market listing by selling shares

u8l1-3.explanation: You make money from what the company pays out (dividends) and from the rise in price (capital gains). Coupons belong to bonds.

u8l1-4.prompt: When you buy Inditex shares on the stock market, that money goes to Inditex.
u8l1-4.explanation: Normally you pay another investor who's selling. The company only receives money when it issues new shares, as in its IPO or a capital increase.

u8l1-5.prompt: You bought a share at €40. Today it's worth €46 and this year you've received €1 in dividends. What's your total return?

u8l1-6.prompt: Are you an owner (share) or a lender (bond)?
options: You get your money back on a set date
You receive dividends if the company pays them
You make a lot if the company grows a lot
u8l1-6.explanation: A shareholder shares in the business's success and risk; a bondholder gets what was agreed if the company can pay.

u8l1-7.prompt: If a company goes bust, shareholders get paid before banks and bondholders.
u8l1-7.explanation: They get paid last, after all the creditors, and almost never get anything back.

u8l1-8.prompt: According to Bessembinder (2018), out of some 26,000 US stocks between 1926 and 2016, what share generated all of the market's net gain?
u8l1-8.explanation: Just 4 % accounted for the entire net gain, and more than half returned less than Treasury bills. That's why a single share is risky and it pays to diversify.

u8l1-9.prompt: Shares are also known as equities, or variable income.
u8l1-9.explanation: What you make isn't fixed in advance: it depends on how the company does.

u8l1-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes: you own a minuscule part of the business, with its profits and its risks
No, you've just bought a number that goes up and down
Yes, and now you can call the shots at the company
u8l1-10.explanation: A share is real ownership of part of the business, however tiny.
feedback: That's it! One in millions, but yours: if the business does well you'll notice, and if it does badly, too.
The price moves every day, but behind it there's a real business you own part of.
You can vote at the AGM, but your vote weighs what your shares weigh: very little.
lines: I've bought 1 share in a video game company 🎮
Does that mean I'm already a bit of an owner?

u8l2-1.prompt: What rights does being a shareholder give you? Select all that apply.
options: Getting your money back on a fixed date
u8l2-1.explanation: Getting your money back on a fixed date is a feature of bonds: shares have no maturity.

u8l2-2.prompt: Match each right with its type.
options: Voting on the board of directors
Buying before anyone else in a capital increase
u8l2-2.explanation: Economic, voting and information rights, plus pre-emptive rights so you don't lose your percentage.

u8l2-3.prompt: At the general meeting, how much does your vote normally weigh?
options: The same as a big fund's
According to what you paid for each share
According to the number of shares you hold
u8l2-3.explanation: As a general rule, one share = one vote. Whoever has more shares has more votes.

u8l2-4.prompt: A small company has 4 million shares and you have 20,000. What percentage of the votes do you have?
u8l2-4.explanation: 20,000 ÷ 4,000,000 = 0.005 → 0.5 % of the votes (if all shares carry voting rights).

u8l2-5.prompt: If you only have a few shares, you have no right to vote at the general meeting.
u8l2-5.explanation: All shareholders with voting rights can vote or appoint a proxy. Some companies require a minimum number of shares to attend in person, but you can vote remotely or group together with others.

u8l2-6.prompt: Pablo has 50 shares in a listed company. He gets the notice of the general meeting: there's a vote on a big pay rise for the CEO. What does he do?
options: Sells all his shares in protest
Nothing: with 50 shares his vote doesn't count
Reads the proposal and votes or appoints a proxy remotely
u8l2-6.explanation: Voting or appointing a proxy is how you exercise your voting rights; listed companies make remote voting easy.
feedback: He can, but he gives up his share of the business over one vote without having used his voice.
His vote doesn't weigh much, but it counts, and if he doesn't vote, others decide for him.
Good: it's his right as an owner, and meetings are decided by adding up big and small votes.

u8l2-7.prompt: Listed companies must report inside information to the ____ so that everyone learns about it at the same time.
u8l2-7.explanation: The Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores supervises the Spanish stock market and publishes that information for free.

options: Being able to buy new shares before others in a capital increase, so you don't lose your percentage
Voting twice at the general meeting
Getting the dividend before other shareholders
u8l2-8.explanation: If the company issues new shares, existing shareholders can buy first in proportion to what they hold.

u8l2-9.prompt: What can the general meeting of shareholders decide? Select all that apply.
options: Setting the share price on the stock market
u8l2-9.explanation: The price is set by the market through supply and demand, not by the meeting.

u8l2-10.prompt: A share has no maturity date.
u8l2-10.explanation: Unlike a bond, a share exists for as long as the company does (or until you sell it).

u8l3-1.prompt: Put a dividend's dates in order.
u8l3-1.explanation: First it's announced; from the ex-dividend date the share trades without the right; then they check who the shareholders are (record) and finally it's paid.

u8l3-2.prompt: By what day at the latest do you need to hold the share to get the dividend?
options: The day before the ex-dividend date
The record date, even if you buy on that same day
u8l3-2.explanation: If you buy on the ex-dividend date or later, the share is already trading without that dividend.

u8l3-3.prompt: A share is trading at €20 and tomorrow is the ex-dividend date for a €0.50 dividend. Roughly what price will it open at, if nothing else changes?
u8l3-3.explanation: 20 − 0.50 = €19.50. The price drops by roughly what leaves the company.

u8l3-4.prompt: A €30 share pays a €1.20 dividend a year. What's its dividend yield?

u8l3-5.prompt: You have 200 shares and each pays a €0.50 dividend. With 19 % withheld, how much reaches your account?

u8l3-6.prompt: Receiving a dividend makes you richer instantly.
u8l3-6.explanation: The price drops by roughly what you receive: your wealth barely changes, and on top of that the dividend is taxed.

u8l3-7.prompt: This is the share of a utility known for paying regular dividends. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u8l3-7.explanation: A company paying a dividend doesn't make its short-term price predictable: the dividend is part of the total return, not a guarantee.

u8l3-8.prompt: Bruno sees a share with a 14 % dividend and wants to put all his savings into it. What would you do in his shoes?
options: Buy right now, 14 % is a bargain
Look into why the price has fallen and whether profits cover the dividend
Buy just before the ex-dividend date, collect and sell
u8l3-8.explanation: Dividend yield rises when the price falls; sometimes it signals problems at the company.
feedback: If the market expects a cut, the dividend may drop and the price fall even further: the 14 % was an illusion.
Good: a dividend like that is often an alarm bell. If profits don't cover it, it'll probably be cut.
The price drops by roughly the dividend on the ex-dividend date and you pay tax on top: there's no free money.

u8l3-9.explanation: That's why, if the price falls, the dividend yield «rises» even though the company isn't paying any more.

u8l3-10.prompt: In Spain, what withholding is normally applied to dividends?
u8l3-10.explanation: The payer withholds 19 % on account of IRPF (Spanish income tax). Dividends then go into the savings tax base, taxed at 19 % to 30 %.

u8l4-1.prompt: You have 10 shares at €400 and the company does a 4-for-1 split. How many shares do you have afterwards?
u8l4-1.explanation: 10 × 4 = 40 shares at €100 each: you still have €4,000.

u8l4-2.prompt: You have 1,000 shares at €0.20 and there's a 1-for-10 reverse split. What price will each new share trade at, if nothing else changes?

u8l4-3.prompt: After a 10-for-1 split you're ten times richer.
u8l4-3.explanation: You have ten times as many shares, each at a tenth of the price: the total value is the same.

u8l4-4.prompt: A company has 100 million shares and you have 1 million (1 %). It raises capital with 25 million new shares and you don't buy any. What percentage do you have now?

u8l4-5.prompt: Match each operation with what happens.
u8l4-5.explanation: Splits and reverse splits don't change the value of your position; capital increases and scrips do change the company's total number of shares.
right: New shares and new money for the company
You choose to be paid in cash or in new shares

u8l4-6.prompt: Why does a company usually do a split?
options: To make each share cheaper and more manageable
u8l4-6.explanation: No money comes in and the company's value doesn't change: only the price of each share falls.

u8l4-7.prompt: What happens to your percentage of the company?
options: Capital increase you don't take part in
Capital increase where you buy your full entitlement
u8l4-7.explanation: Only a capital increase you don't take part in dilutes you. If you exercise your pre-emptive rights, you keep your percentage.

u8l4-8.prompt: A reverse split usually follows good news for the company.
u8l4-8.explanation: It doesn't change the value, but it's usually done by companies that have fallen a lot and trade for cents.

u8l4-9.prompt: Quick: 2-for-1 split of an €80 share. New price?
u8l4-9.explanation: 80 ÷ 2 = €40, and you have twice as many shares.

u8l4-10.prompt: Marta sees in her app that one of her shares «has fallen 90 % today». She had 5 and now 50 show up. What's happened?
options: The company has given her 45 shares
There's been a 10-for-1 split and her money is worth the same
u8l4-10.explanation: Before panicking over a huge drop, check whether there's been a split.
feedback: Nobody gives anything away: it's the same pizza, cut into more slices.
Exactly: from 5 to 50 shares at a tenth of the price. The total value doesn't change.
It would be with the same number of shares, but now she has ten times as many.

u8l5-1.prompt: A company trades at €50 and has 200 million shares. What's its market cap?

u8l5-2.prompt: Match each size with its approximate market cap (convention in dollars).
u8l5-2.explanation: These are rough ranges used by indices and fund managers; there's no single official cut-off.

u8l5-3.prompt: Match each index with what it measures.
u8l5-3.explanation: There are indices for every size: that way you can compare how they perform.

u8l5-4.prompt: What does a small company usually have compared with a giant?
options: More growth potential and more risk
u8l5-4.explanation: It can grow faster, but its price moves more and it goes bust more often.

u8l5-5.prompt: A €2 share belongs to a small company and a €500 share to a large one.
u8l5-5.explanation: A share's price tells you nothing about size: you have to multiply it by the number of shares.

u8l5-6.prompt: Large or small? Work out the market cap.
u8l5-6.explanation: 20,000 M, 1,000 M, 15,000 M and 1,000 M. Price on its own tells you nothing.

u8l5-7.prompt: Ana wants to put all her savings into a micro cap a forum is talking about: «it could go up 10 times». What does she bear in mind?
options: That if it's on a forum it's been properly analysed
That it's very volatile and illiquid, she could lose almost everything and it's unwise to bet it all on one company
That small caps always rise more
u8l5-7.explanation: More potential always comes with more risk, and putting everything into one small company multiplies it.
feedback: Forums are also the favourite hangout of people who want to pump up a share so they can sell it.
Good: the potential is real, but the risk of a single small company is enormous.
Sometimes they rise more, but many fall by the wayside or go bust.

u8l5-8.prompt: Quick: how is market cap calculated?
u8l5-8.explanation: It's the company's value on the stock market.

u8l5-9.prompt: Small-cap shares usually have wider spreads than large caps.
u8l5-9.explanation: There are fewer buyers and sellers, so buying and selling costs more.

options: No, small caps never go up
Yes, in the long run they always win
They can return more, but with more risk, and it's not a fixed rule
u8l5-10.explanation: Size changes the risk profile, but it doesn't guarantee a result.
feedback: Some small caps become giants; the hard part is knowing which ones in advance.
Not always: there have been periods of many years in which large caps clearly beat them.
That's it! More potential, more scares and years when they do worse.

So I'm moving everything into small caps 🚀

u8l6-1.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning.
u8l6-1.explanation: Two styles, a tool to measure them and a trap worth knowing about.
right: Cheap because the business is getting worse
You buy current earnings at a discount
You pay today for future earnings

options: Mature utility with a P/E of 11 and a steady dividend
Bank trading below its book value
P/E of 60 on expectations for a new product
Young tech company doubling sales and paying no dividend
Reinvests all its profit to expand
u8l6-2.explanation: Growth: high P/E, little dividend and lots of reinvestment. Value: low P/E, mature business and a dividend.

u8l6-3.prompt: A share trades at €100 and earns €2 per share. What's its P/E?
u8l6-3.explanation: 100 ÷ 2 = 50: you're paying for 50 years of current earnings.

u8l6-4.prompt: March 2000: the Nasdaq 100, packed with growth tech stocks, has multiplied more than 4 times since the end of 1997. What happened next?
u8l6-4.explanation: With sky-high P/Es, the price depends on very demanding expectations being met. It's a classic case for studying growth and valuation.

u8l6-5.prompt: This is the share of a classic value company: mature, consumer goods, and paying a dividend for decades. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u8l6-5.explanation: Being a stable company doesn't make its short-term price predictable: value shares go up and down too.

options: A cheap share that keeps falling because its business is deteriorating
A fund that charges hidden fees
u8l6-6.explanation: A low P/E may reflect that profits are about to fall: sometimes cheap is cheap for a reason.

u8l6-7.prompt: Growth shares usually pay high dividends.
u8l6-7.explanation: They reinvest almost all their profit to keep growing.

u8l6-8.explanation: The P/E measures how many years of current earnings you're paying for.

u8l6-9.prompt: Laura can't decide between a tech company with a P/E of 70 growing 40 % a year and an insurer with a P/E of 9 growing 3 %. Which reasoning is right?
options: The P/E 9 one is better because it's cheap
The P/E 70 one is better because it grows more
Neither is better on its own: it depends on whether the price properly reflects its future
u8l6-9.explanation: Neither «it grows a lot» nor «it's cheap» is enough: you have to compare the price with what the company can earn.
feedback: It may be cheap for a reason: a stagnating business disappoints too.
If that growth is already in the price, any disappointment can sink it.
Exactly: growth and value are styles, not guarantees. What matters is what you pay for what you get.

u8l6-10.prompt: Which style suffers more if expected growth disappoints?
u8l6-10.explanation: With a high P/E, the price already reflects future earnings; if they don't arrive, the P/E deflates.

u8l7-1.prompt: What does a company do in a share buyback?
options: Buys its own shares and usually cancels them
u8l7-1.explanation: When they're cancelled, there are fewer shares and each one is worth a bigger part of the company.

u8l7-2.prompt: A company earns 500 million and has 100 million shares. It buys back and cancels 10 million. New earnings per share? (two decimal places)
u8l7-2.explanation: 500 ÷ 90 = €5.56, versus €5 before: 11 % more with the same profit.

u8l7-3.prompt: You hold 1,000 of a company's 1,000,000 shares (0.1 %). It buys back and cancels 200,000. What percentage do you have now?
u8l7-3.explanation: 1,000 ÷ 800,000 = 0.00125 → 0.125 %. Your stake grows without you buying anything.

u8l7-4.prompt: Buying back shares always creates value for shareholders.
u8l7-4.explanation: If the company buys back at a very high price or borrows to do it, it can destroy value.

options: You pay no tax until you sell
Taxed in the year you receive it
u8l7-5.explanation: Both return money to shareholders, but in different ways and with different tax treatment.

u8l7-6.prompt: Match each use of profit with its effect.
u8l7-6.explanation: A company can pay out, buy back, reinvest or pay down debt: each option makes sense at a different moment.
right: Fewer shares and a bigger slice for each

u8l7-7.prompt: A company announces a big buyback funded by a loan, right when its share is at an all-time high with a very high P/E. How do you see it?
options: With caution: price and debt matter
u8l7-7.explanation: A buyback is only as good as the price it's done at and how it's paid for.
feedback: Buying back expensively and with debt can destroy value: it pays a lot for each share and adds risk.
Good: a buyback creates value if it's done at a good price and without putting the company at risk.
They're legal and common; in the US they've been subject to a 1 % tax since 2023.

u8l7-8.prompt: When bought-back shares are cancelled, the total number of shares falls.
u8l7-8.explanation: That's why each share represents more profit.

u8l7-9.explanation: Net profit ÷ number of shares. A buyback raises it because the denominator falls.

u8l7-10.prompt: Why do some investors prefer buybacks to dividends?
options: Because they're not taxed until you sell
Because Hacienda (the Spanish tax office) pays for them
u8l7-10.explanation: A dividend is taxed when you receive it; with a buyback, your gain builds up in the price and you pay when you sell.
